doc.title: Types
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script can annotate variables, function parameters and returns, and local type names with Adaptive data types and simple structured types. Leaves are registered data types such as integer, string, boolean, object, array, any, and void.

These annotations are part of the script language. They are separate from adaptive object types and property meta used by adapters and requests. Object-type rules at the adapter and request layer are unchanged. Script type and interface declarations define shapes used only for script type checking.
Railroad diagrams below match the harvested grammar productions. For the complete syntax, see the .

section.title: Type
section.paragraph: A Type is a union of intersection types (see below). That is the top production used wherever a type is written: after : on bindings and parameters, in type aliases, and in object and function type forms.
Older spellings such as (array of integer) or (object "…") are not accepted.

section.title: Example
TypeName and DataType
section.paragraph: A primary type is a type name, an object type literal, a tuple, or a parenthesized or function type. A type name is either an Adaptive data type id or a name declared with type / interface in the script.

section.title: Example
ArrayType
section.paragraph: Write an array of element type T as T[]. Multiple [] suffixes nest (for example integer[][]). There is no separate Array<T> form; use T[] only.

section.title: Example
TupleType
section.paragraph: A tuple type lists element types in order inside [ … ]. Length and each position matter when the value is known (for example a list literal).

section.title: IntersectionType
section.paragraph: An intersection type is one or more array types joined with &. A value must satisfy every arm.

section.title: Example
UnionType
section.paragraph: A union type is one or more intersection types joined with |. A value may match any arm.

section.title: Example
section.code: const u: integer | string = 1; const v: integer | string | boolean = true;

section.title: ObjectTypeLiteral
section.paragraph: An object type literal lists named properties with types. A trailing ? after a property name marks it optional. Property names may be identifiers or string literals. A property that holds a function is written with a function type after the colon (for example run: (a: integer) => integer), not with a method-style signature.
This is a script shape only. It does not import an adaptive object type from an adapter catalog.

section.title: Example
FunctionType
section.paragraph: A function type describes a callable value: (parameters) => Return. Parameters may be named with optional ? and rest ..., or written as bare type names. A parenthesized type that is not a function type is still a parenthesized Type.
Script function values use function (…): Return (colon before the return type). That is the value form; the type annotation form uses =>.

section.title: Example
OptionalType and OptionalReturnType
section.paragraph: An optional type is a leading : and a Type. That form appears on const / let bindings, pattern leaves, parameters, and similar places. Optional return type is the same idea on a script function declaration. : void marks a procedure (the call does not complete), not ECMAScript’s empty-function undefined.

section.title: Example
Type statement
section.paragraph: type Name = Type; declares a local alias for a type. The name may then be used as a type name in the same script unit. A name must already be declared (or be an Adaptive data type), except that a type may refer to itself in its own body (type Node = { next?: Node }). A type that only aliases itself (type A = A, or a cycle of aliases through | / & only) is an error. An unknown type name is always a compile error.

section.title: Example
section.code: type Id = integer; const x: Id = 3;

section.title: Interface statement
section.paragraph: interface declares a named object shape. Use extends for one or more base interfaces. Optional properties use ? after the property name.

section.title: Example
Type checking (default off)
section.paragraph: Type annotations are always accepted by the compiler. Checking is off by default so existing scripts keep working. Turn checking on with environment flags, or with a #compile pragma in a script.

Flags may be set from the host environment or with flag_set in a script. When compile checking is on, calls to known Adaptive functions are checked at compile time against each function’s parameter and return types when those types can be determined without running the call. That includes function parameters that take a function (for example a predicate), when the argument is a known script function.
These flags control type checking for scripts compiled while they are set:

list.item: compile:typeCheck — check at compile time when types are known, and at runtime on assignment and script function parameters
compile:typeCheckCompileOnly — compile-time checks only (used instead of full typeCheck when both are set)
compile:noImplicitAny — when checking is active, a missing annotation is an error instead of any
compile:strictNullChecks — stricter handling of null and undefined
compile:strict — turns on typeCheck, noImplicitAny, and strictNullChecks together

section.paragraph: In a script you may write #compile followed by one or more options and a semicolon. Options use the name after compile: (case-sensitive). A #compile pragma overrides the environment flags for that script only; it does not change the environment flags used by other scripts.
Options you can write after #compile:

list.item: typeCheck — same as compile:typeCheck
typeCheckCompileOnly — same as compile:typeCheckCompileOnly
noImplicitAny — same as compile:noImplicitAny
strictNullChecks — same as compile:strictNullChecks
strict — same as compile:strict
noOptimize — same as compile:noOptimize (evaluate without the usual value optimizations; mainly for core debugging)
noTypeCheck — turn type checking off for this script (does not turn off noOptimize)

section.paragraph: You may combine options in one statement (spaces between them, no commas), for example #compile typeCheck noImplicitAny;.

A #compile statement may appear anywhere a statement is allowed. It applies from that point on in the same script. Constructs already parsed before the pragma are not re-checked under the new options.

section.title: Example
What is checked
section.paragraph: When checking is on:

list.item: Data type leaves (for example integer versus string).
Unions and intersections.
Array types: the value must be an array; element types are checked when the value is known (for example an array literal).
Tuples: length and each position when the value is known.

Object and interface shapes: required properties must be present; property values must match their types; extends bases are included. An object literal may not include properties outside the type (including when used as a function argument). Object literals with spreads or computed property names skip that extra-key check. At runtime, values that are not object literals may still have extra properties, so adaptive objects can be wider than the script type.
Function return types when a return type is declared.
Function types: script functions and closures are checked for parameter and return compatibility; other function values only need data type function.
Calls to a known script function (by name, or through a const binding that holds a function with a known type) check arguments against parameter types when those types are known.

Calls to known Adaptive functions check arguments and arity when types are known, including Adaptive functions that take a function argument (for example a filter predicate) when the argument is a known script function.
Array and object patterns: annotations on individual bindings such as const [a: integer] = … or { host: h: string } are enforced when those bindings receive values.

section.paragraph: Bindings without an annotation, and data that arrives from outside the script, are treated as any at compile time unless noImplicitAny is set. Runtime data type and adaptive object-type rules still apply on their own.
Checking only runs where types can be determined without evaluating unknown expressions. Values that stay any or unknown are not forced to invent a type at compile time.
